text: Instagram is an American photo and short-form video sharing social networking service owned by Meta Platforms. It enables users to upload media that can be edited with filters, organized by hashtags, and geotagged with a location. Posts can be shared publicly or with preapproved followers, and users can browse content by tags and locations, view trending content, like photos, and follow others to include their content in a personal feed. Available on iOS, Android, Windows 10, and the web, Instagram supports 33 languages including English, Hindi, Spanish, French, Japanese, and Korean. The platform began as Burbn, a mobile check-in app developed by Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger, which was first released as a web-based prototype on October 21, 2009, with a registration waiting list. The first Burbn post was a photo of South Beach Harbor at Pier 38, posted by Mike Krieger on July 16, 2010, at 5:26 p.m. On October 6, 2010, the Burbn Beta app was made available for iOS through the App Store as a prototype, receiving around 25,000 registrations. Six days later, on October 12, 2010, the final stable non-beta version was officially released under the new name Instagram. The app rapidly gained popularity, reaching 1 million registered users in two months, 10 million in a year, and 1 billion by June 2018. In April 2012, Facebook (now Meta Platforms) acquired Instagram for approximately US$1 billion in cash and stock, with the deal closing on September 6, 2012, at a purchase price of $300 million in cash and 23 million shares of stock. The acquisition was approved by Britain's Office of Fair Trading on August 14, 2012, and by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission on August 22, 2012. Mark Zuckerberg stated Facebook was committed to building and growing Instagram independently. Instagram initially used Foursquare API for location tagging, switching to Facebook Places in March 2014. In 2015, the desktop interface was redesigned to be more flat and minimalistic, with one row of pictures reduced from five to three to match the mobile layout, and the slideshow banner was removed. In April 2016, Instagram released a Windows 10 Mobile app, and a desktop app for Windows 10 personal computers and tablets followed in October 2016. The Windows 10 Mobile app was discontinued on April 30, 2019, though the mobile website remains as a progressive web application. In May 2016, Instagram introduced a black-and-white flat design theme and a more abstract, colorful icon. In December 2016, Instagram introduced comment liking, where users can like comments without receiving notifications. In April 2018, Instagram introduced data download capabilities to comply with GDPR regulations. IGTV launched on June 20, 2018, as a standalone video app and was shut down in March 2022 due to low usage and a shift to short-form video. On September 24, 2018, Krieger and Systrom announced they would step down, and Adam Mosseri became the new head of Instagram. In May 2019, Instagram began piloting the removal of publicly displayed like counts, initially in Canada, later expanded to six other markets and globally in November 2019, with the goal of reducing user anxiety about likes and encouraging deeper connections. In August 2019, Instagram piloted the removal of the "Following" tab, which was made official in October, as the feature was underused and some users were surprised by its visibility. Instagram later restricted public profile viewing, requiring users to log in after viewing a limited number of posts. In the same month, Instagram launched Threads, a messaging and video chat app similar to Snapchat, integrated with the "Close friends" feature and including photo editing tools, but discontinued it in December 2021 due to low usage and feature overlap. In March 2020, Instagram launched "Co-Watching," allowing users to share posts during video calls to meet social distancing demands. In August 2020, Instagram pivoted to video with the introduction of "Reels" to compete with TikTok, and added suggested posts based on user interests. In February 2021, Instagram tested Vertical Stories and began testing the removal of feed post sharing to stories. In March 2021, Instagram launched a feature allowing four people to go live simultaneously and introduced a child safety policy restricting adults from messaging teens they don't follow. In May 2021, users in some regions could add pronouns to their profile. On October 4, 2021, Meta suffered its worst outage since 2008, affecting Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp, with experts identifying a possible DNS-related issue. On March 17, 2022, Zuckerberg confirmed plans to add non-fungible tokens (NFTs) to the platform. In April 2022, Instagram tested removing the ability to see recent posts from hashtags, which became permanent a year later, limiting hashtags to curated content from top users, a move aimed at reducing misinformation and in response to claims that hashtags do not help posts gain views. In September 2022, Ireland's Data Protection Commission fined Instagram $402 million for privacy violations involving minors. In December 2022, Instagram introduced Notes, a feature allowing users to share short text posts of up to 60 characters with specific people, who can reply via messaging. In February 2023, Instagram enabled users to browse and post GIFs in comments and announced Meta would sell blue "verified" badges on Instagram and Facebook. On July 5, 2023, Meta launched Threads as a social network connected to Instagram, allowing public shortform posts of text, photos, and videos, and enabling conversations and reblogging, aiming to compete with Twitter. In December 2023, Instagram launched a podcast titled "Close Friends Only" featuring celebrity conversations, with the first episode featuring Ice Spice and Doja Cat, and subsequent episodes in June and August 2024 featuring Reneé Rapp, Rachel Sennott, Megan Thee Stallion, and GloRilla. In April 2024, Instagram announced plans to test tools to combat sextortion. On August 2, 2024, Turkey blocked Instagram after the platform deleted posts from users offering condolences for the death of Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh. In December 2024, Instagram and MTA collaborated to sell Metrocards featuring creators such as New York Nico, Overheard In New York, and SubwayTakes. On September 3, 2025, Instagram launched a native iPadOS app, which previously relied on the iOS app and did not utilize the larger screen size of tablets. Users can upload photographs and short videos, follow other users' feeds, geotag images with a location, set their account as private to require follower approval, and connect their Instagram account to other social networking sites.

In April 2024, Instagram announced it would begin testing new tools within weeks to combat sextortion, a form of blackmail involving the distribution of intimate images online. On August 2, 2024, Turkey blocked Instagram after the platform removed posts from users offering condolences for the death of Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh. In December 2024, Instagram and MTA partnered to sell Metrocards featuring creators such as New York Nico, Overheard In New York, and SubwayTakes. On September 3, 2025, Instagram launched a native iPadOS app, which previously relied on the iOS app and did not utilize tablet screen sizes. Users can upload photos and short videos, follow others' feeds, and geotag images with location names. Accounts can be set to "private," requiring approval for new follower requests. Users can link their Instagram account to other social platforms to share content. In September 2011, a new app version introduced live filters, instant tilt–shift, high-resolution photos, optional borders, one-click rotation, and an updated icon. Photos were initially limited to a 1:1 square aspect ratio; since August 2015, the app supports portrait and widescreen formats. A map of geotagged photos was removed in September 2016 due to low usage. Since December 2016, posts can be saved in a private area; in April 2017, users could organize saved posts into named collections. Users can also archive posts in a private storage area, out of public view, to prevent deletion of photos with low likes or deemed boring, and to reduce the "emergent behavior" of deleting content. In August, Instagram introduced comment threading to improve user interaction. Since February 2017, up to ten photos or videos can be included in a single swipeable carousel post, initially limited to square format, later updated in August to support portrait and landscape. In April 2018, Instagram launched "focus mode," a portrait mode that blurs the background while keeping the subject in focus. In November 2021, Instagram began supporting Alt text for photos to assist visually impaired users, either generated via object recognition or manually added by uploaders. On March 1, 2021, Instagram Live Rooms enabled four people to go live together. In May 2021, closed captions were introduced for videos on Instagram Reels and Stories. In January 2011, hashtags were introduced to help users discover photos and each other, with encouragement to use specific and relevant tags. Users have created trends through hashtags, such as #SelfieSunday, #MotivationMonday, #TransformationTuesday, #WomanCrushWednesday, #ManCrushMonday, and #ThrowbackThursday. In December 2017, users could follow hashtags to see curated highlights; the ability to search "Recent" hashtags was temporarily disabled during the 2020 U.S. elections to prevent misinformation, tested again in 2022, and removed entirely in April 2023, leaving users with only a curated selection of "popular" posts. In June 2012, Instagram introduced the "Explore" tab, which displays popular photos, nearby location content, and search results; updated in June 2015 to include trending tags, places, curated content, and location search; in April 2016, a "Videos You Might Like" channel was added, followed by an "Events" channel in August featuring live event videos, and Instagram Stories in October; in November 2016, after Instagram Live launched, the Explore tab included a curated page of the best live videos; in May 2017, it promoted public Stories from nearby places. Instagram offers various filters, including a "Lux" filter added in February 2012 that lightens shadows, darkens highlights, and increases contrast, and five new filters—Slumber, Crema, Ludwig, Aden, and Perpetua—added in December 2014. Initially a photo-sharing service, Instagram introduced 15-second video sharing in June 2013, seen as a response to Vine; in August 2015, it added support for widescreen videos; in March 2016, the video limit was increased to one minute; albums were introduced in February 2017, allowing up to 10 minutes of video in one post. IGTV, a vertical video app launched in June 2018, allows uploads of up to 10 minutes (650 MB) with verified users able to upload up to one hour (5.4 GB); videos play automatically upon launch, a feature contrasted by CEO Kevin Systrom to video hosts requiring video location; the app was shut down in March 2022. Edits is a video editing app available on Android and iOS, featuring AI tools, direct posting to Instagram or Facebook, video statistics, and trending content in the Inspiration tab; announced on January 19, 2025 in response to U.S. government actions against TikTok and CapCut, available for pre-order on iOS in January 2025 with an Android launch in February 2025 and initial iOS release on March 13, 2025, officially released for both iPhone and Android on April 21, 2025. Instagram Reels is a short-form video section of Instagram, focusing on vertical videos under 90 seconds with interactive features; as of November 2024, it averages 150 billion daily views, with creators earning money based on views or ad revenue. Reels was first rolled out to Brazil in November 2019, then expanded to France and Germany; officially launched in Pakistan in August 2022, two years after its global rollout in August 2020; functions similarly to TikTok, allowing users to create short videos using existing sounds from other clips, with initial limits of 15 seconds (later 30); uses existing Instagram filters and editing tools. In July 2020, Reels was rolled out to India after TikTok was banned; in August 2020, it launched in 50 countries including the U.S., Canada, and the U.K.; in August 2020, a Reels button was added to the home page. On June 17, 2021, full-screen sponsored ads were introduced in Reels, up to 30 seconds with a "sponsored" tag; despite Meta's spending to attract creators, user engagement lagged behind TikTok as of 2022; in June 2022, Reels duration was increased to 90 seconds; in January 2025, a three-minute duration was announced after testing. A 2021 study by Devadas Menon identified seven motivations for Reels usage: socially rewarding self-promotion, entertainment, escape, surveillance, novelty, documentation, and trendiness; it found that narcissists showed higher usage, socially rewarding self-promotion and entertainment predicted creation and participation, escapers showed higher consumption and participation, and entertainment seekers created more videos and participated actively; the study confirmed "lurking," where users only watched content without creating or participating. On February 26, 2025, users reported a sudden surge of violent and graphic content in their Reels feeds; Meta issued a public apology, stating a technical error caused the unintended recommendation of such content and confirmed the error was fixed. Since 2020, Reels usage has grown; in September 2022, it generated over 140 billion daily views; monthly users increased from 1.5 billion in 2022 to 1.8 billion by 2024. Researchers from Guizhou University of Finance and Economics and Western Michigan University found that short-form videos like YouTube Shorts, TikTok, and Instagram Reels may contribute to addictive behavior in young adults and children due to "short bursts of thrills"; college students in the U.S. and China use them for entertainment, knowledge, and social identity building. The Wall Street Journal reported parental concerns about short-form videos, noting no way to disable Instagram or set limits; children learn to expect constant stimulation and fast changes, which can impair focus on activities like reading. Studies highlight a connection between short-form videos and the brain's reward system, specifically dopamine release; Dr. Anna Lembke, a psychiatrist, noted that brief, attention-grabbing videos trigger dopamine surges similar to addictive behaviors; the rapid, easily consumable nature of these videos elicits high dopamine levels, leading to compulsive seeking and addictive patterns, resulting in shorter attention spans and slower cognitive processing. In December 2013, Instagram launched Instagram Direct, enabling private messaging (DMs) with photos and videos between users who follow each other; messages from non-followers are marked as pending and require acceptance; users can send photos to up to 15 people. In September 2015, Direct received a major update with conversation threading, allowing sharing of locations, hashtag pages, and profiles directly from the feed; users can reply with text, emoji, or a heart icon; a camera within Direct lets users take and send photos without leaving the conversation. In November 2016, users could make private messages disappear after viewing, with a notification if a screenshot is taken. In April 2017, Direct was redesigned to combine all messages—permanent and ephemeral—into single threads. In May 2017, users could send website links and photos in original portrait or landscape orientation without cropping. In April 2020, Direct became accessible on the Instagram website via WebSocket technology. In August 2020, Facebook began merging Instagram Direct into Facebook Messenger, with the Instagram Direct icon changing to the Facebook Messenger icon. In March 2021, a feature was added to prevent adults from messaging users under 18 who do not follow them as part of child safety policies. In August 2023, Instagram introduced privacy adjustments allowing users to receive only one direct message from non-followers, requiring approval before further messages; this can be changed to allow unlimited messages from non-followers. In September 2024, Instagram added a sticker editor enabling users to cut out photo elements and send them privately, as well as add stickers and write on photos. In August 2016, Instagram launched Instagram Stories, allowing users to take photos, add effects and layers, and post them with a 24-hour expiration; the feature was noted to resemble Snapchat. CEO Kevin Systrom acknowledged the criticism of copying Snapchat but stated that features like Stories were developed to address limitations such as inability to pause or rewind; he noted Snapchat originally lacked filters, which Instagram had introduced earlier. In November 2016, live video functionality was added to Stories, allowing users to broadcast live with videos disappearing immediately after. In January 2017, Instagram launched skippable ads, where five-second photo and 15-second video ads appear between content.

Instagram's features and developments have evolved significantly over time, drawing on elements from other social platforms like Hipstamatic, Twitter, and Facebook, such as the "Like" button, with Systrom noting that every feature can be traced back to earlier technological history. He compared the similarities between Instagram and Snapchat to the auto industry, emphasizing that multiple platforms can coexist with distinct features serving different audiences. Instagram adopted Stories to address user frustrations with the inability to pause or rewind content, implementing these features after Snapchat introduced filters, which Instagram later copied. In November 2017, Instagram added live video to Stories, with the broadcast disappearing after ending; in June 2017, users could save live videos to their Stories for up to 24 hours or discard them immediately. In July 2017, users could respond to Stories with photos and videos, including filters, stickers, and hashtags. Stories became accessible on mobile and desktop websites in late August 2017. On December 5, 2017, Instagram introduced "Story Highlights," or "Permanent Stories," which do not expire and appear below the profile picture and biography, accessible on desktop. By June 2018, Instagram had 400 million daily active story users and 1 billion monthly active users. In December 2024, Instagram trialed a feature showing unseen Story Highlights at the end of the Stories tray, only displaying curated Highlights and not standard Stories, requiring users to view all current Stories first, which may be challenging for those with many followers. In September 2025, Instagram began testing a Reels-first interface in India and South Korea, placing Reels as the default home tab, with Stories at the top and DMs in the center; the Reels tab is second, with a new Following tab offering "All," "Friends," and "Latest" feed options. Meta launched paid verification in 2021, allowing users to pay for a blue verified badge, which signifies authenticity and credibility, appearing as a blue checkmark in search results, profile pages, and comments. Verification was initially granted by Instagram for public interest accounts, but in August 2018, users could apply directly. The badge requires meeting criteria such as being notable, authentic, unique, complete, and compliant with community guidelines, though not all applicants are verified. Emily White joined Instagram as Director of Business Operations in April 2013, stating the company would begin selling ads by September 2014, and left in December 2013 to join Snapchat. James Quarles became Global Head of Business and Brand Development in August 2014. In October 2013, Instagram announced video and image ads for U.S. users, with image ads launching on November 1, 2013, and video ads on October 30, 2014. Ads expanded to the U.K., Canada, and Australia in June 2014, rolling out that autumn. Carousel ads were announced in March 2015, launched in October 2015 for images, and in March 2016 for video. By February 2016, Instagram had 200,000 advertisers, increasing to 500,000 by September 2016 and 1 million by March 2017. In May 2016, Instagram launched tools for business accounts, including business profiles, analytics (Instagram Insights), and ad promotion, requiring a linked Facebook page; Insights first launched in the U.S., Australia, and New Zealand, expanding globally in 2016. In November 2018, business accounts could add product links to direct users to purchase pages or save to a shopping list. In April 2019, "Checkout on Instagram" allowed merchants to sell directly through the app. In March 2020, Instagram announced moderation changes to reduce disinformation about COVID-19, removing such accounts from recommendations, downranking false content rated by third-party fact-checkers, and limiting false content in Explore. In June 2021, Instagram launched a native affiliate marketing tool, with posts labeled "Eligible for Commission," partnering with Sephora, MAC, and Kopari. Instagram released three standalone apps: Bolt in July 2014, a disappearing image messaging app; Hyperlapse in August 2014, an iOS-exclusive app creating time-lapse videos; and Boomerang in October 2015, a video app combining photos into one-second back-and-forth loops. Microsoft released a Hyperlapse app for Android and Windows in May 2015, but Instagram has not released an official app for those platforms. Third-party services integrate with Instagram for content creation, print generation, analytics, and alternative clients, especially for platforms with no official support, such as iPads. In November 2015, Instagram ended feed API access effective June 1, 2016, to maintain community control and create a sustainable environment for authentic experiences, and prohibited third-party clients from using "insta" or "gram" in their names. These changes aimed to prevent replication of the Instagram experience and combat abuse from automated click farms and account hijacking, with further API restrictions introduced after the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Third-party services allow unlimited browsing of public profiles and anonymous viewing of Stories, which are considered more authentic due to their 24-hour disappearance (though users can see who viewed them for 48 hours), making them valuable for market research. On December 16, 2019, Facebook expanded its fact-checking program to Instagram, using third-party organizations to identify, review, and label false content, removing such content from Explore and hashtag pages and labeling it as false; image matching technology was used to detect duplicates. In April 2016, Instagram changed the photo order in the timeline from chronological to algorithm-driven, prioritizing content from users liked by the viewer, which drew significant backlash, with users requesting notifications and the company refusing to reverse the change or provide an option to revert it, reaffirming this in 2020. In December 2021, Adam Mosseri stated the company was developing a chronological feed, introducing two modes: a classic chronological feed and a version where users select "favorite" accounts whose posts appear at the top in chronological order, with others mixed below. Since 2017, Instagram has used "shadowbanning" to reduce the visibility of accounts generating non-genuine engagement or spam, including excessive hashtags, and has been accused of extending this to censor sexually suggestive content under vague circumstances. The December 2018 update, which attempted to shift the feed from vertical to horizontal scrolling via swiping left to mimic Stories, caused user outrage, with Instagram later calling it a bug or accidental test deployment. In November 2020, Instagram replaced the activity feed with a "Shop" tab and moved the activity feed to the top, relocating the "new post" button to the top and replacing it with a Reels tab, stating the Shop tab improves brand and product discovery and Reels helps users discover short videos. However, users criticized the change, with The New York Times calling Reels "confusing, frustrating and impossible to navigate." In 2020, Instagram introduced "suggested posts," adding content from accounts the algorithm believes users would like, which drew controversy from The Verge, which claimed it would keep users glued to the feed, increase advertising space, and harm mental health, while Instagram executive Julian Gutman denied this intent. The feature faced more criticism when Fast Company reported it could not be turned off. On June 23, 2021, Instagram tested moving suggested posts ahead of posts from followed accounts, citing positive reception. In 2021, The Wall Street Journal obtained internal Meta research showing that Instagram worsens body image in young people, particularly girls, with one in three teenagers affected, 20% feeling worse about themselves and 40% better, 70% of teen girls and 40% of teen boys experiencing negative social comparison, and Instagram having a greater impact on appearance comparison than TikTok or Snapchat. 13% of British and 6% of American teens with suicidal thoughts could trace their thoughts to Instagram use. Instagram responded by stating the findings were limited and presented negatively, and Meta defended the confidentiality of the research as promoting internal dialogue. In response to the backlash, Meta paused development of Instagram Kids, stating it was reviewing concerns from regulators and parents. Khodarahimi & Fathi (2017) found evidence that users displayed higher levels of depressive and anxious symptoms.

Instagram has been linked to negative effects on body image, particularly among young people, with girls being especially vulnerable. One in three teenagers report negative impacts on their body image due to Instagram, with 20% feeling worse about themselves and 40% feeling better. Seventy percent of teen girls and 40% of teen boys experience negative social comparison, and research indicates Instagram has a greater impact on appearance comparison than TikTok or Snapchat. Among users with suicidal thoughts, 13% of British and 6% of American teenagers could trace their thoughts to Instagram use. Instagram responded to criticism by stating its findings were based on a limited set of data and presented in a negative light, while Meta defended the confidentiality of its research as a way to foster internal dialogue. In response to backlash, Meta paused the development of Instagram Kids and stated it was reviewing concerns from regulators and parents. Studies show that users exhibit higher levels of depressive and anxious symptoms compared to non-users, and browsing content predicts depressive symptoms, though liking and posting do not. Viewing celebrity and peer images can negatively affect women’s moods, and users with a strong need for approval are more likely to falsely present themselves, increasing depression risk. Following more strangers increases social comparisons and depressive symptoms, and increased time on Instagram correlates with higher anxiety. Users report greater body surveillance, appearance-related pressure, eating-disorder-related pathology, and lower body satisfaction than non-users. Those who take more selfies and edit them strategically show higher body dissatisfaction and lower self-esteem, and editing selfies can reduce facial satisfaction. Comments on appearance lead to greater body dissatisfaction. Mackson et al. 2019 found Instagram users report less loneliness, and a 2021 study showed not being tagged in photos causes social exclusion, especially for those with high need-to-belong. Brailovskaia & Margraf 2018 found a positive link between Instagram use and extraversion, life satisfaction, and social support, with only a marginal negative link to self-conscientiousness. Women who took a seven-day break from Instagram reported higher life satisfaction than those who continued using it, with no such difference observed in men. The relationship between Instagram use and fear of missing out (FOMO) is confirmed in multiple studies, and browsing predicts social comparison, which generates FOMO and can lead to depression. Boys with accounts show over-evaluation of shape and weight, skipping meals, and disordered eating cognitions, while girls show only skipping meals and stricter exercise schedules. Appel et al. 2016 and Feltman et al. 2017 found a positive link between intense Instagram use, body surveillance, and disordered eating. Picardo et al. 2020 found self-harm posts had negative emotional effects on some users, with evidence of online content affecting offline behavior, though no causality was claimed. Instagram offers resources for users in need of support. Sharenting—parents posting about their children—is common on Instagram, with over 10 million images under the hashtag #letthembelittle, many containing personal details like names, ages, and locations. Sanz-Blas et al. 2019 found users who report spending too much time on Instagram show higher "addiction" levels linked to stress, and Foroughi et al. 2021 found desire for recognition and entertainment predict Instagram addiction, which negatively affects academic performance. Gezgin & Mihci 2020 found frequent Instagram use correlates with smartphone addiction. After its October 2010 launch, Instagram reached one million users by December 2010, 5 million in June 2011, 10 million in September 2011, 30 million in April 2012, 80 million in July 2012, 100 million in February 2013, 130 million in June 2013, 150 million in September 2013, 300 million in December 2014, 400 million in September 2015, 500 million in June 2016, 600 million in December 2016, 700 million in April 2017, and 800 million in September 2017. In June 2011, Instagram passed 100 million photos uploaded, reaching 150 million by August 2011, and over 50 billion photos by June 2023. Instagram Stories reached 100 million active users in October 2016, 150 million in January 2017, 200 million in April 2017 (surpassing Snapchat), and 250 million in June 2017. Instagram Direct had 375 million monthly users in April 2017. As of 2014, 50% of users used iPhone and 50% used Android; 68% of users are female and 32% male. Instagram use favors urban areas, with 17% of U.S. urban adults using it versus 11% in suburban and rural areas. Despite being a major photo-sharing platform, only 7% of daily photo uploads among top platforms come from Instagram. It attracts younger users, with 90% of its 150 million users under 35. From June 2012 to June 2013, user numbers approximately doubled. Income-wise, 15% of U.S. users earning under $30,000, 14% earning $30,000–$50,000, and 12% earning over $50,000 use Instagram. Education-wise, 23% of users with some college education are active, followed by 18% college graduates and 15% with a high school diploma or less; 24% use the app several times a day. Media content with faces receives more likes and comments, and filters that increase warmth, exposure, and contrast boost engagement. Users engage more with images of fewer individuals and unwatermarked content. Instagram offers a verified badge application, though not all applicants receive it. Young people primarily use Instagram to view posts for social interaction and recreation, with lower agreement on creating posts, reflecting its emphasis on visual communication. In June 2020, Instagram became a key platform for social justice movements like Black Lives Matter, though activism has been criticized as performative and overly aesthetic. Instagram uses automated algorithms, user reports, and human review to remove illegal content such as child abuse, terrorism, cyberbullying, hate speech, and misinformation. The U.S. government has little power to force content removal, but Instagram has voluntarily removed content, such as deleting the "recent" tab on hashtag pages in October 2020 to prevent misinformation during the 2020 U.S. election, and banning former President Donald Trump from the platform on January 7, 2021, citing risks during the Capitol attack. Instagram has faced criticism in India for not removing homophobic and transphobic content in Indian languages, despite removing such content in English, and a 16-year-old queer artist died by suicide after receiving thousands of hate comments. Users have posted drug-selling images, leading to the blocking of related hashtags and a dedicated review team; in 2019, Facebook and Instagram banned influencers from promoting vape, tobacco, and weapons. In October 2013, Instagram deleted Canadian photographer Petra Collins’ account for a photo showing minimal pubic hair, which she claimed violated no terms, as the platform’s rules prohibit only "pornographic or sexually suggestive photos," and critics noted inconsistencies in content moderation, such as allowing hashtags like #faketits and #gunsforsale. Similar deletions occurred in January 2015 for a fashion agency and in March 2015 for poet Rupi Kaur’s photos of menstrual blood, sparking a "We will not be censored" campaign. The #FreetheNipple campaign challenged Instagram’s censorship of women’s nipples, though Instagram has not commented extensively; CEO Kevin Systrom cited Apple’s App Store age rating (12+) as justification, though this has been questioned due to inconsistent enforcement and lack of consequences for male nudity. The Iranian government offered up to $9,000 in bribes to delete accounts, targeting Masih Alinejad. After the 2020 assassination of Qasem Soleimani, Instagram removed posts supporting Soleimani, citing U.S. sanctions, a move described as "undemocratic" by officials. In May 2021, during the eviction of Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, users reported content removal, visibility limits, and account restrictions, with Instagram denying intentional censorship and attributing deletions to glitches; digital rights groups argue this reflects digital discrimination and call for transparency. In October 2023, Instagram incorrectly labeled profile bios with the Palestinian flag emoji and "Alhamdulillah" as containing "terrorist" content due to a translation error, apologized, and corrected it. Censorship has occurred in several countries: China blocked Instagram after the 2014 Hong Kong protests, and the Cuban government blocked it during the 2021 protests. Instagram was one of the last freely available global platforms in Iran, seen as a tool for freedom and access to the world, though Iran has imprisoned citizens for posts.

The phrase "Praise be to God" was incorrectly translated by Instagram's automated system as "Palestinian terrorists are fighting for their freedom," an error the platform attributed to its computerized translation system, apologized for, and corrected. Instagram has faced censorship in several countries: China blocked it following the 2014 Hong Kong protests, as Hong Kong and Macau were not affected due to their status as special administrative regions; Cuba blocked access during the 2021 protests to limit information spread; in Iran, Instagram remained one of the last freely available global social media sites, with users viewing it as a tool for freedom and global connection, though the government periodically blocked it during anti-government protests from 2019–20 and in July 2021 censored videos containing the phrase "death to Khamenei," with permanent blocking implemented in September 2022 for both Instagram and WhatsApp, except for tourists and corporations; North Korea blocked Instagram after a fire at the Koryo Hotel on June 11, 2015, to prevent photos from spreading; Russia banned Instagram in March 2022, citing alleged "calls for violence against Russian troops" during the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, affecting nearly 80 million users, and labeled both Instagram and Facebook as extremist, making it illegal to access them via VPN under a law passed on July 17, 2025, with fines of 3,000 to 5,000 rubles (€30 to €50) by September 1, 2025; Turkey banned Instagram on August 2, 2024, after the assassination of Ismail Haniyeh, with the ban lasting nine days and being lifted on August 10, 2024, after Instagram agreed to work with authorities; in the U.S., social media content regulation is minimal, with removals mostly voluntary, except in January 2020 when Instagram and Facebook removed posts supporting Qasem Soleimani to comply with U.S. sanctions; following Donald Trump's 2025 election, some sources noted possible censorship targeting the Democratic Party on Meta platforms. Instagram won "Best Mobile App" at the 2010 TechCrunch Crunchies in January 2011, was named number 66 in Fast Company's "100 Most Creative People in Business" in May 2011, and was included in Inc.'s "30 Under 30" list in June 2011; it won "Best Locally Made App" at the SF Weekly Web Awards in September 2011, was featured on the cover of 7x7 Magazine's "Hot 20 2011" issue, and was named Apple's "App of the Year" in December 2011; in 2015, it was ranked No. 1 by Mashable as one of the 100 best iPhone apps and was listed in Time's "50 Best Android Applications for 2013"; a 2017 UK Royal Society for Public Health survey of 1,479 people aged 14–24 found Instagram to be the worst for young mental health, citing anxiety, depression, loneliness, bullying, and body image, though it also noted positive effects like self-expression and community building; Instagram responded by prioritizing a safe and supportive environment and filters out reviews and accounts that violate community guidelines, with violations leading to bans; in 2017, Harvard and University of Vermont researchers developed a machine learning tool that outperformed general practitioners in diagnosing depression using color analysis, metadata, and face detection; in 2019, Instagram began testing the hiding of like counts, later making it available to all users, and in 2021 reverted to publicly viewable like counts by default, allowing users to disable them per post or for their entire feed; correlations exist between Instagram content and body dissatisfaction due to self-comparison, with half of applicants admitting to photo editing linked to body image concerns; in October 2021, CNN reported on two young women, Ashlee Thomas and Anastasia Vlasova, whose lives were endangered by Instagram's toxic effects on diet; in October 2023, 42 U.S. states sued Instagram and Meta, claiming the platforms contributed to a youth mental health crisis due to addictive design and misleading claims about dangers, with Meta stating disappointment and a desire to collaborate on better standards; Instagram introduced comment controls in July 2016, allowing users to turn off comments and block offensive language, with the feature rolling out to celebrities in early August and regular users in September, and by December, users could also turn off comments and remove followers from private accounts; in June 2017, Instagram implemented an automated comment filter using Facebook's DeepText algorithm to detect offensive, harassing, or spammy comments, with filtering based on user-specified keywords; in September 2017, users could limit who could comment (e.g., only followers or people they follow), and the comment filter expanded to support additional languages; in July 2019, Instagram introduced a system to proactively detect problematic comments and prompt users to reconsider, and allow users to "restrict" others' communication, citing that younger users found the existing block system too extreme; an April 2022 study by the Center for Countering Digital Hate found Instagram failed to act on 90% of abusive direct messages reported to five high-profile women—Amber Heard, Bryony Gordon, Rachel Riley, Jamie Klingler, and Sharan Dhaliwal—despite reports, with Instagram disputing the findings; on August 9, 2012, English musician Ellie Goulding released a music video for "Anything Could Happen" using over 1,200 fan-submitted Instagram photos with filters representing lyrics; in August 2017, a bug in Instagram's developer tools allowed access to contact information (email and phone numbers) of high-profile verified accounts, including Selena Gomez, with the company stating it had fixed the issue and was investigating; more details emerged with hackers selling the data online, affecting "millions" of accounts, with a searchable database posted for $10 per search, and the Verge reporting that cybersecurity firm RepKnight found contact data for actors, musicians, and athletes, including Selena Gomez's account being used to post naked photos of Justin Bieber; Instagram admitted it could not determine which specific accounts were impacted but believed it was a low percentage, though TechCrunch reported six million accounts affected; in 2019, Apple removed an app that scraped Instagram accounts to stalk users; Iran has implemented DPI blocking for Instagram; in September 2024, Meta paid a $101 million fine for storing up to 600 million Instagram and Facebook user passwords in plain text, a practice first discovered in 2019 but reportedly ongoing since 2012; on December 17, 2012, Instagram updated its Terms of Service to allow businesses to pay for the display of users' usernames, likenesses, photos, and actions in sponsored content without compensation, with no opt-out option before January 16, 2013, leading to severe user backlash; Instagram CEO Kevin Systrom responded by removing the controversial language, clarifying that the intent was to experiment with innovative advertising, not to sell photos, and committed to updating the policy for clarity; the backlash prompted competing photo services to promote privacy-friendly alternatives, gaining user growth; on December 20, 2012, Instagram reverted the advertising section to its original October 2010 version, though the original policy already granted Instagram the right to use user content in ads; the policy update included an arbitration clause, which remained after the advertising language was revised; Columbia Law School professor Tim Wu has claimed Facebook's 2012 acquisition of Instagram was a felony, citing a memo from a senior Facebook official stating the acquisition was to eliminate a potential rival, a violation of U.S. antitrust law, with Wu noting the email was from Mark Zuckerberg; Instagram was used for propaganda purposes during the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine to promote certain domestic goals or foreign policy objectives.[523] The most-liked photo on Instagram is a carousel featuring footballer Lionel Messi celebrating after winning the 2022 FIFA World Cup, which has received over 76 million likes.[526] In 2022, Instagram was the second most downloaded mobile app of the year.[527] The platform is developed using Python, and its artificial intelligence features content description for visually impaired users who rely on screen readers.[528][529]
